Numbers collected recently by Beauhurst as an update to 
last year’s Seeding to Succeed report show only a minimal 
increase in terms of the number of first-time seed-stage 
deals done, but a significant increase in terms of the 
overall amount raised in such deals. While it’s good to see 
that more capital is finding its way to new businesses, this 
growth is not big enough compared to what we’re seeing in 
later-stage venture capital. More importantly, not enough 
companies are receiving seed investment. It looks that 
most businesses created in 2020 failed to attract initial 
funding. Investors concentrated on backing only a small 
group of new businesses, and this might be a sign of more 
aversion to risk and a dangerous trend that is contrary to 
growth in general. 
 
In order to maintain strong funding of innovation at later 
stages, seed-stage funding has to be double or triple that 
at the later stage—both in terms of number of deals and 
amount of investment. Funding via SEIS and EIS is crucial 
to ensure this, and cannot be underestimated. 
 
These days the UK is facing a new set of financial 
challenges: a cocktail of the Brexit implementation period, 
a crisis around the cost of living, geopolitical tensions, and 
post-pandemic recovery. Young companies, which are agile 
and ambitious in nature, can play a vital role in meeting 
these challenges. This might be directly, by innovating 
solutions to newfound problems or changes in the way we 
live and work, or indirectly through the value generated by 
their rapid growth, seen in job creation and tax receipts. 
 
This means that the seed stage is a critical part of the 
entrepreneurial ecosystem and needs greater support. 
Over the last decade, SEIS has had a transformative impact 
on the availability of funding for seed-stage companies—
by offering tax reliefs to individual investors it has allowed 
young businesses to flourish. This is a phenomenon we 
need to see continuing as startups meet the UK’s new 
financial challenges; SEIS and EIS should be used as a tool 
to incentivise essential capital circulation in the economy 
that will fund them. 
Moving forward, we can expect that newly-formed 
businesses will generate a number of innovative products 
and services focused on social sustainability, climate 
change, or other ESG concerns. Despite increasing interest 
in these areas, many investors remain reluctant to back 
such businesses, especially in their early stages, believing 
there will be lower returns. SEIS and EIS funding will again 
be important here, encouraging investors to back these 
young businesses when they are newly trading. This will 
enable them to grow, make an impact, and be ready for 
follow-on investment down the line.

First-time deals and SEIS
In 2021, the number of 
initial deals in the seed-
stage increased while the 
number of second deals 
and beyond declined, 
drawing the two figures 
close to converging again. 
The pandemic and changes 
to both everyday life and 
business activities triggered 
a flurry of innovation; the 
2021 increase in seed-stage 
initial deals may be a sign 
of investors beginning to be 
ready to tap into this new 
entrepreneurship. 
 
This early-stage funding is 
vital for young businesses 
to start growing. Early 
finance allows companies 
to work on product 
development, conduct 
market research, and take 
on their first key staff. 
Initial investment into new 
businesses as the economy 
began its recovery in 2021 
was and remains vital.

Seeding to Succeed: 2021 Update
Seeding to Succeed: 2021 Update
2022 prognosis
Although the year-on-year decline in the number of 
first-time seed-stage investments has stopped, it is 
important to note that the growth between 2020 and 
2021 has been modest. The data suggests that the 
number of companies that receive investor money at 
the seed stage is plateauing, a worrying trend that must 
be reversed in order to nurture the next generation 
of innovative startups. Seed-stage investment needs 
to be comfortably higher than later-stage in order to 
keep innovation fuelled throughout the ecosystem. 
A record number of new companies—781,000—
were started in 2020, with 2021 close behind. As 
these companies mature, they will start to seek 
external finance to fuel their growth. Of the 494,000 
businesses incorporated in 2012, 1,568 raised equity. 
At the same rate, 2,479 of 2020’s new companies will 
raise funds. With this promising tailwind of potential 
demand from new companies, some of them bringing 
important solutions to the market, it’s crucial to ensure 
the right level of funding supply. The top organised 
investors into first-time deals in 2021 are all continuing 
to invest in 2022 (and beyond). A key factor, however, 
will be supporting the use of the SEIS scheme by 
individual investors—who often underpin the funds 
deployed by institutional investors. As we have 
noted before, individuals are the seed investors most 
susceptible to change in the macroeconomic climate: 
putting £150,000 into an early-stage company requires 
great confidence. At the same time, the typical first-
time investment of £150,000 is not enough anymore 
to support progress—the times have changed, 
inflation is driving up prices and the costs of running 
a business, and startups from the US, the EU, and 
China attract higher tickets and are more comfortable 
penetrating international markets. Already in 2022 
the macroeconomic headwinds are blowing hard, so 
uncertainty remains around these deals. Therefore, 
it is more critical than ever that young companies are 
supported in their scaling journey. We have already 
tracked nearly 100 first-time deals in January, and are 
still finding more—it is essential to keep sight of the 
necessity of SEIS to the innovation ecosystem going 
forward. SEIS, as well as EIS, the tested and proven 
tools of investing in innovation, have to be reinvented, 
improved, and reinforced before it is too late.
Beauhurst is a searchable database of the UK’s high-growth companies. Our platform is 
trusted by thousands of business professionals to help them find, research and monitor 
the most ambitious businesses in the UK. We collect data on every company that 
meets our unique criteria of high-growth; from equity-backed startups to accelerator 
attendees, academic spinouts and fast-growing scaleups.
Our data is also used by journalists and researchers who seek to understand the high-
growth economy, and powering studies by major organisations—including the British 
Business Bank, HM Treasury and Innovate UK—to help them develop effective policy.
